section_name: What Is Informative Writing — Overview and Common Genres
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Informative Writing Essentials

The first 2 episodes addressed the importance of establishing a regular writing routine where direct mini-lesson instruction is followed by independent practice.

Now, in Episode 3, the focus is specifically on the mini-lesson skills that we are to teach within informative writing units. Depending on your state standards, you may be teaching informative, explanatory, or expository writing. Regardless of the terminology, this type of writing focuses on teaching the reader about a topic or text. Common examples of this include:

- Writing Summaries that highlight only the big ideas and most important information.
- Explanations that answer a specific question.
- Letters that communicate information to an individual, organization, or business.
- Step-by-step directions that provide a sequenced set of information.
- Research that reports factual information drawing on multiple sources.
- Essays that dive into a broad topic, providing abundant information.
- And Compare-contrast writing that presents information about two or more topics or texts.

Now your state standards likely don't name these different types. Rather they more broadly outline that you are to teach students HOW to write in 3 different MODES — persuasive, informative, and narrative.

Each of these modes comes in many different forms or GENRES. Simply change the writer's purpose, and a business letter INFORMING the audience could become a business letter PERSUADING the audience, an informative research report could become an argumentative research paper, and an informative essay could become a narrative one. What's changing is NOT the genre or type of writing, but the MODE or purpose. Just as we read for different purposes, we write for different purposes. And our standards indicate that we have to teach students HOW to persuade, inform, and entertain within their writing.

section_name: Four Essential Informative Writing Skills — Introduction and Primary Grades
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Four Essential Informative Writing Skills

Throughout this third episode, Kristina Smekens dissects four essential informative-writing skills that we need to teach our elementary writers.

Before identifying them, she addresses those who teach in the primary grades or those working with students who haven't yet mastered sentence writing. You may not immediately see the connection, but you too can achieve this same informative writing expectation.

Consider a nonfiction author who produces a wordless book with only photographs. That IS informative writing, as we learn a lot about the topic through visuals only. Now consider a MOSTLY wordless book that includes photos labeled with key vocabulary or simple phrases. That's informative writing too. We learn about the topic through the visuals and the words and details that label them.

While we do have to teach students how to write sentences, the informative writing standard does not reference any sentence-level skills. There's no mention of complete sentences, capitalization, punctuation, grammar, mechanics, or spelling in any of these. Teaching informative writing is NOT dependent on students writing sentences.

BUT what does stand out are 4 common ingredients that appear ACROSS the grade-level expectations. These indicate that informative writing includes:

1. Introducing the topic or text.
2. Providing LOTS of facts and details.
3. Organizing the information.
4. Concluding or closing the writing.

As we move UP the grade levels, additional skills appear, BUT these four are the core. These are the foundational skills that we should build our elementary informative writing units around. These four require direct, explicit, mini-lesson instruction — regardless if your students are writing in pictures or sentences.

section_name: Skill #1 — Introduce the Topic (Across Grade Levels)
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #1: Introduce the Topic

We know that strong writing includes a beginning, middle, and end. And when teaching students how to START an informative piece, the writer needs to identify the topic for the reader: "What are you going to teach us about?"

At the intermediate level, this often begins as a single sentence introduction. It's one sentence that names the topic.

Before students can write sentences independently, I would still teach them to introduce their topic to the reader, but to do it via a 1 or 2 word title. This title serves as the introduction when students aren't yet writing sentences. But, when they are, they can build on this skill, stretching the topic into a complete thought — an introductory sentence.

As we continue to move DOWN the grade levels and the developmental stages, I would STILL teach young writers that they have to reveal the topic to the reader, and they can do this via a picture — with or without a label. Model how to point at the picture they drew and orally state the topic in a sentence. Kids who learn to SAY a topic sentence, eventually learn to WRITE one — and that's what we're doing, building a scaffold of grade-appropriate informative writing skills.

Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #1: Upper Elementary Introduction (Whole Paragraph)

We've looked at introductions in the lower grade levels, now let's move UP and past merely writing a single sentence. The expectation for upper elementary is usually a more sophisticated beginning — a whole paragraph. This requires direct instruction on WHAT else to include in the beginning — besides the topic sentence.

Start these mini-lessons by reminding students that the writer's purpose in informative writing is to TEACH and EDUCATE the reader on a topic. But they have to assume that their reader knows NOTHING. So, before revealing the topic sentence, the writer might:

- Provide 1-2 sentences of background information on the bigger subject or concept.
- OR, if the piece is about a text, the writer should name the text AND SUMMARIZE it in 1-2 sentences.
- OR, if the topic includes any key words or unfamiliar vocabulary, then the writer might identify and define those terms for their reader.
- And if the writer is comparing & contrasting 2 topics or texts, then he should FIRST introduce each one separately — in its own sentence — before revealing in the topic sentence that you will compare them.

A strong beginning is NOT about the number of sentences written in the first paragraph. It's about teeing up the topic for the reader so he can then learn lots of important facts and little details about it.

In addition to NAMING or introducing the topic, students need to learn that informative writing is HEAVY in facts and information.

section_name: Skill #2 — Facts and Details (Primary: Drawing and Labeling)
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #2: Provide Facts and Details (Primary Grades)

This ties back to the writer's purpose. In order to TEACH our readers, we can't be general or vague about the topic. And again, this isn't just a skill we teach AFTER students are able to write words and sentences.

We teach our youngest writers how to draw what they know about the topic — to communicate their understanding through picture details. Within these mini-lessons, model the importance of including close-up & tiny details about the topic. Just as important as providing MANY details, the writer has to include ACCURATE ones. Describe the writer as the teacher, he is TEACHING the READER about this topic, and it has to be the CORRECT information.

This requires mini-lessons on how to draw accurate sizes & shapes, and the value of using true-to-life colors in our pictorial writings. If the topic is a person, teach students how to draw people with shapes, rather than stick people. Explain that they can convey MORE information about the topic by adding clothing and accessories that accurately depict this individual. And when students are ready to include even more details in their informative drawings, teach them how to add facts about the environment, the setting, or the habitat where this topic resides.

Remember, all this pictorial writing we are doing is only temporary. What we are really teaching students is HOW to communicate INFORMATIVELY even before they can write letters, words, and sentences. Then, WHEN phonics and sentence-sense kick in, students already know the important ingredients relevant within ALL informative writing.

While we're not aiming to create artists, the act of drawing does prove that the student is thinking. He is demonstrating that he KNOWS about the topic. AND, the more the student draws with details, the more he'll be able to label.
skill_title: Facts and Details (Primary: Drawing and Labeling)

section_name: Skill #2 — Facts and Details (Labeling, Word Choice, and List Writing)
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #2: Labeling and List Writing

Teach students how to sound-stretch and label the NUMEROUS close-up details they included within their drawings.
- This usually begins with NOUNS — labeling people, places, and parts relevant to the topic.
- Then push for MORE details. Remind them that writers want to INFORM the reader on EVERYTHING that they know about this topic. This includes writing labels that include expert vocabulary and domain-specific terms.
- Keep going! Teach students how to include adjectives before the nouns, creating 2-word labels. Color words, sensory details, descriptions — these are part of strong informative writing at every level.
- And so are verbs! Provide mini-lessons on how to label the movements and actions of different objects within the drawing.

Remember, drawing & labeling are only temporary stages of writers. What we are teaching is that ALL informative writing includes many details about a topic and relies on precise word choice and specific description. Kids who learn to draw and label detailed pictures will transfer that same understanding when writing multiple sentences within informative paragraphs.

As we move through the developmental writing stages, deliver similar mini-lessons, teaching students how to make a LIST of everything they know about the topic — including related details about people, places, things, names, numbers, descriptions, adjectives, nouns, and verbs.

List writing requires application of phonics, spelling, letter formation, and spacing. BUT it DOESN'T overwhelm the student with capitalization, end marks, and text wrapping expectations, too. So when list-writing, students can focus on communicating lots of information while practicing only SOME conventions.

THEN, with their details listed, students can turn their focus to stretching the words and phrases into sentences.
skill_title: Facts and Details (Labeling, Word Choice, and List Writing)

section_name: Skill #2 — Elaboration Types for Intermediate Grades
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #2: Elaboration for Intermediate Grades

Now, in the intermediate grade levels, the expectation of writing with lots of details increases dramatically — from multiple sentences to multiple PARAGRAPHS. This is most successful with a 2-step process. FIRST, teach students to identify the key points or main parts of the topic. (Now some students will think they're done at this point. They assume the reader will fill in the blanks — that "he knows what I mean.") However, each of these general ideas needs to be explained thoroughly. Teach students to think of EACH main point as a topic sentence needing its own paragraph.

Again this requires direct mini-lesson instruction on HOW to develop an idea — What to SAY about that key point. And the same TYPES of details taught in the lower grades are applicable in the upper grades.

- Specific details come in the form of names. Teach students to identify specific examples, types, brands, breeds, and proper nouns.
- Include precise numbers — like quantities, dates, times, measurements, percentages, and more. Including these specifics make the reader see the writer as credible and knowledgeable on the topic.
- Description isn't its own mode of writing — it's a characteristic of ALL writing. Provide mini-lessons on how to weave in relevant description among all of those facts. Teach students how to utilize precise adjectives and action verbs to create a visualization for their readers.

In addition to all of these, teach intermediate students NEW types of details, too.
- Like how to do more than just KERPLUNK big words into their informative writing. Again, remind them of their reader, and that they DO want to utilize expert vocabulary, BUT they ALSO have to include simple definitions or explanations. If they don't, the reader feels left out or worse, confused.
- Additional mini-lessons may also teach older students how to select valuable text evidence in order to bolster their message. Model how to quote only the strongest sentence — versus dumping in large chunks of text — OR how to paraphrase an author's idea to state it more succinctly.

Often students DO KNOW more about the topic, but they don't demonstrate it within their generic sentences and skimpy paragraphs. What we need to teach them are WAYS to say more — what TYPES of details they can add. When we do this, their writing tends to EXPLODE with more specifics.

Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #3: Organize the Information

ALL informative writing requires direct instruction on how to INTRODUCE the topic AND develop it with facts & details. The 3rd essential skill targets the organization of the writing.

This skill seems fairly straight forward — "The details have to be organized." BUT it's more complex than it appears. It requires teaching students the 3 most common ways to organize their informative writing:

- In a Chronological SEQUENCE
- Within CATEGORICAL groups
- Or using categories of COMPARISON

After pushing students to include more information, we inadvertently create a new problem: a lack of organization. And this usually occurs because they are inserting details as they think of them while writing the first draft.

Rather, teach students how to just LIST the known facts and details FIRST. Then, how to group related details together. Do this in 2 separate steps and BEFORE they begin the first draft. For example:

- If writing a how-to (like directions or a procedure) or explaining a process, system, or the evolution of something, then the students FIRST list everything they know about the topic. THEN, they group related details into a chronological SEQUENCE. Everything that happens first is explained in the first body paragraph. All the details related to what happened second are grouped within the second body paragraph, and so on.
- OR, after listing everything the writer knows about a topic, he groups details to reveal the different parts, components, or facets. Each group of details will produce a paragraph, with the label that holds them together being the topic sentence.
- And if comparing two topics or texts, the writer lists everything known about them INDIVIDUALLY FIRST. Then identify categories that exist within both. For example, if comparing seasons, then clothing, weather, food, and outdoor activities might be the categories. If comparing literature, then character, setting, plot, and theme are typical.

section_name: Skill #3 — Organization Across Grade Levels and Assessment
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #3: Organization Across Grade Levels

Teaching students HOW to organize information is extremely difficult, which is WHY most K-2 writing standards do NOT include it as a skill for primary STUDENTS to master. However, as our young writers include MORE and MORE details, it will become a necessary ingredient to introduce. Consequently, K-2 teachers should be prepared to PROVIDE the categories or the main points of a writing topic. Allow students to first draw and write the different facts and details — each on separate paper or sentence strip. Then, ask them WHICH ONES are all about X? Which ones teach the reader about Y?

Show students how to arrange and tape the pages or sentences together to create organization in the middle.

While primary teachers PROVIDE the categories, this is a skill that intermediate teachers have to eventually release to the students. This is something THEY have to master independently. In fact, organizing all the details is typically assessed within state writing tests. When rubric criteria measures if the student "wrote a response in the correct text structure" or "organized the information in the right genre," they are assessing a student's ability to organize information logically.

A meaty AND organized middle is important. But we don't want students to simply STOP at the end of the middle or worse, write THE END, THANK YOU, GOODBYE.
skill_title: Organization Across Grade Levels and Assessment

content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Skill #4: Writing a Conclusion

This leads to the fourth essential skill — teaching students HOW to write an ending for any informative piece. Again at different grade-levels and developmental stages, the conclusion will look and sound different.

- Lower grade-level standards require that we teach students to provide a sense of closure by restating the topic or topic sentence. This connects the ending to the beginning. YOUNG writers should be taught to do this orally — even before they are writing words and sentences.
- A slightly more sophisticated conclusion is to reiterate the topic sentence using synonyms and a different sentence structure.
- Beyond that, a traditional summary is usually suggested, which includes a restatement of the topic sentence and a review of the main points discussed in the middle. HOWEVER, when attempting to further advance your writers, the summary conclusion can seem robotic and repetitive — especially if the middle wasn't very long. "The reader didn't forget what it was about. He doesn't need to be reminded."

The thing is, conclusions don't follow a recipe. In fact, the final sentences of an informative piece can EVEN reveal NEW information.

Teach students how they could:
- Offer the reader some good news within the conclusion. This works well when the topic is negative, harsh, severe, or just heavy. Good news may include an unseen advantage or benefit, a little hope or encouragement related to the topic.
- Another option would be to teach students how to synthesize all the middle details using the SO-WHAT approach. "So you said all this information in the middle — so what? What's your point? What is the last thing you want to say to the reader about this topic?" These questions are a springboard for the writer to consider a final thought.

Good News and So What endings often generate a powerful, voice-filled closing thought, although it may be just one sentence. BUT this IS acceptable. The standards for informative writing recognize that the conclusion can be a section OR a statement, a paragraph or a single sentence. The strength of an ending isn't based on the number of sentences it contains, but in how effectively it brings the topic to a close.

section_name: Episode Takeaway — Prioritize the Four Essential Informative Skills
content:
Episode 3 Elementary — Takeaway

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the most important takeaway: That we must teach students the UNIQUE ingredients inherent within informative writing. THIS is what the standards expect of us — ALL of us, at every grade level.

So I encourage you to review your lessons and make adjustments in order to prioritize these 4 standards-based informative-writing skills.

By targeting these essential skills when teaching informative writing, we take the next step toward building better writers.
skill_title: Prioritize the Four Essential Informative Skills
